newsitem.title: USA: TEXT-U.S. District Court Conrail opinion.
newsitem.headline: TEXT-U.S. District Court Conrail opinion.

text.p: Following are excerpts of U.S. District Court Judge Donald Van Artsadlen's opinion on Tuesday denying a request by Norfolk Southern Corp to block the intended merger of CSX Corp and Conrail Inc .

In the case, Norfolk Southern alleged Conrail's board of directors violated their corporate duties under Pennsylvania law in agreeing to the merger and stiff break-up provisions. Norfolk Southern is pursuing a rival bid for Conrail, announced after the merger with CSX was announced.
The U.S. Third Circuit Court of Appeals said Wednesday it would consider Norfolk Southern's request that it hear an appeal of the decision.
In the decision, read from the bench Tuesday night and made available on transcript Wednesday, Van Artsdalen said,

-- On the actions of Conrail's board: "There has not been shown any type of lack of good faith...Although there may be some argument that the directors should have made some further inquiry, they have the right to rely on recommendations of corporate officers and those who negotiate on their behalf."

-- On board discretion under Pennsylvania law: "I think that it is clear from the Pennsylvania statutes, which are not ambiguous...that it is up to the board of directors and they alone, so long as they act in good faith after reasonable investigation, as to what is in the best interest of the corporation."

-- On the responsibilities of board members: "Directors may consider all groups that may be affected by their actions, including shareholders, employees, customers, communities...and may consider both the short-term and the long-term interests of the corporation."
"Directors are not required to consider the interest of any group, obviously including shareholders, as a dominant or controlling factor."
-- On directors' role in considering takeover bids:
"The directors have every right to favor one competing bid over another, and particularly have the right to resist hostile takeovers..."

"The Pennsylvania statutes...were enacted...in order to exclude (decisions in Delaware law) that seem to mandate or suggest that the primary or perhaps only consideration in a (takeover) situation...is what is the best financial deal for the stockholders in the short term..."

"Although these decisions may be fine for the shareholders whose only interest is that of a short-term financial investment...it completely ignores the economic utility and value of corporations as a form of business enterprise that produces goods and services for the public and the national economy...Directors have the right to consider these matters."

-- On Norfolk Southern allegations that the two-tiered CSX bid would coerce stockholders into accepting a bid they would otherwise reject: "I do not see any coercion, but several options, any of which will undoubtedly end up being a net return to most shareholders far in excess of whatever their original investment may have been."

-- On Norfolk Southern's suggestion that CSX be restricted from voting, in a Conrail vote enabling the merger, shares it acquires in a tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail's stock. "All shareholders, if they are shareholders of record...have the right under the law to vote on that matter."

-- On Norfolk Southern charges that Conrail was motivated by CSX guarantees of succession to Conrail Chairman David LeVan and board spaces for Conrail directors: "I see nothing wrong with the merger agreement providing who will be the main executive officers for the first years after the completion of the merger."
